essays.title: if (document.layers): the web forks in two
essays.description: In 1997 Netscape and Microsoft each invented their own model of a web page. Everyone wrote every effect twice, and the way it ended explains a lot about how the web still works.
unverified: That the "Best viewed with" buttons were usually 88 by 31 pixels. The buttons are well documented; I did not open a source for the size.
The mention of Dynamic Drive as a source of copy-and-paste scripts. Its site would not load when this was checked.
Why the two browsers exposed such different models. The engine explanation is my best guess, and the essay says so.

essays.title: Where did all the old web developers go?
essays.description: Around 2008 nobody writing JavaScript seemed to be over 40, and the industry spent a decade arguing about why. The answer was arithmetic, and the same arithmetic is running again.
unverified: Vivek Wadhwa's 2010 TechCrunch piece and the original 2009 "Plan B" essay are named from secondary references. I did not open either directly.
The Stanford and ADP employment figures are quoted from SoftwareSeni's summary, not from the study itself.
The CNBC figure on senior job postings is quoted from Fullstack's summary of CNBC's reporting.
That the staff and principal engineering track spread through the 2010s is my reading, not a sourced claim.

essays.title: getYear() and the year 19100
essays.description: One small Date method returned 100, 2000 or 100 again for the year 2000 depending on the browser, got fixed three different ways, and is still in every browser today.
unverified: The January 2000 sightings of "19100" (the US Naval Observatory, Meteo-France, the Gore campaign site) rest on Wikipedia's Year 2000 problem article, not on the original news reports.
Internet Explorer 9's return to "year minus 1900" in standards mode rests on one reference page.
JDK 1.1 is dated only to February 1997, because sources disagree on the day.
Whether Navigator 4.0 to 4.05 returned 100 or 2000 could not be pinned down, so the essay speaks only about 4.06 and later.
Why Navigator 3 changed the method is my guess, and is marked as one.

essays.title: jQuery 1.0: what $ really replaced
essays.description: jQuery 1.0 shipped in August 2006 with a dollar sign borrowed from another library, and replaced a folder of copy-pasted fixes that its own author had been winning contests with.
unverified: When the "write less, do more" slogan first appeared. It is sourced only to Wikipedia's citation of the jquery.com page title.
The date of the first release. The jQuery project says January 14, 2006; John Resig's own write-up implies the 15th. The essay reports both.
Whether the jquery-1.0.js file on the jQuery CDN is identical to the one released on August 26, 2006. Its header carries an October 2006 revision date.
Why jQuery 1.3.2 used querySelectorAll only for document-rooted queries is my inference.
John Resig's age at the time comes from Wikipedia.

essays.title: View Source was the school
essays.description: For about fifteen years the web trained its own workforce through one menu item that showed how any page was made, and then the pages stopped being readable.
unverified: Netscape's exact menu labels and keyboard shortcut for viewing source. The essay says only that the name varied by browser and year.
Tim O'Reilly's essay is linked in its print view, because the canonical page refused to load.
That the Firefox bug reporter copied the script from a page's source is an inference, and is worded as one.
Why Internet Explorer opened source in Notepad rests on a single 2008 Microsoft blog post.

essays.title: Firebug: the first look inside the page
essays.description: In January 2006 one developer uploaded a few days of code as a Firefox add-on, and within a few years every browser had copied its panels, its F12 key and its console.log.
unverified: Joe Hewitt's own 2006 blog posts. His site is down, so his words are quoted only as they appear in Mozilla Hacks and a FOSDEM interview.
The January 12, 2006 announcement date comes from Jay Hoffmann's history of the web, and is flagged in the text.
That F12 as the developer-tools key began with Firebug 0.2.3 rests on Wikipedia, and is attributed to it.
The Firebug 1.1 source listings come from a third-party mirror, which the essay names.

essays.title: XMLHttpRequest: six years waiting for a name
essays.description: Microsoft shipped the object behind every web application in 1999, under a name its author calls an excuse. Almost nobody used it until a designer's 2005 essay called the technique Ajax.
unverified: Almost everything about how XMLHTTP was written and shipped rests on one account, Alex Hopmann's. He gives no date for the weekend, the naming or the security review beyond starting the webmail work "probably sometime in late 1998", and his page shows no original publication date.
Jesse James Garrett's essay is linked as a saved copy of its print view, because Adaptive Path's own site would not load.

The dates for Mozilla, Safari 1.2 and Opera 8.0 support come from Wikipedia, as do Oddpost's 2002 opening and the release months of Internet Explorer 5 and 7. Wikipedia's XMLHttpRequest article also dates the idea to 2000, which contradicts Hopmann; I followed Hopmann.
Jay Hoffmann's history of the web says XMLHTTP was added to replace Java components that Outlook Web Access had relied on. Hopmann does not mention this, so I left it out.

How little the object was used before 2004 is hard to measure. Aaron Swartz wrote that nobody he knew used it, but Hopmann says the approach was already doing well by 2000 to 2002, and it was common on corporate intranets.
Google's two blog posts are linked for their dates only. Whether Google Maps used XMLHttpRequest or hidden frames at launch is disputed in the comments on Swartz's post, so the essay does not say.

That XMLHTTP sitting behind ActiveX held back public sites, that Prototype's wrapper kept most developers from typing the constructor, and that the missing name mattered as much as I say, are my own readings.

essays.title: The webmaster: a mailbox that became a job
essays.description: "Webmaster" was coined as a mail alias on a style page, grew into the title for whoever ran the whole site, and faded, while the address in the footer link outlived the job.
unverified: That "webmaster" was coined on the etiquette page rests on Tim Berners-Lee's own note on that page. The 1993 date is my inference from a November 1992 snapshot without the word and Merriam-Webster's first-use year.
That the W3C folder named MailArchive/webmaster holds mail sent to the webmaster address is my reading of its name and of the greeting in one message. The archive itself does not say.
The 1996 Web Week survey is quoted from an undated Princeton Review career profile. I could not find the survey itself, and Georgia Tech's webmaster surveys from the same years would not load.
Louise Addis as the first webmaster, and the reasons the role faded, rest on one secondary source, Jay Hoffmann's history.
Google's 2008 "Webmaster Team" and webmaster job ladder rest on one person's blog post.
Microsoft's advisory on the live.fi certificate does not name the mailbox that was registered, so the essay does not either.
That address harvesting drove webmasters to scripts and forms is supported only by Wikipedia and by RFC 2142's warning. The FTC's 2002 study of harvesting would not load, so it is not cited.
The four forces behind the one-person job, and the comparison of the server administrator with an on-call rotation, are my own readings.

essays.title: The IE6 funeral: campaigning to kill a browser
essays.description: In March 2010 a Denver web shop buried Internet Explorer 6 in a pine coffin and Microsoft sent flowers. The browser had a fifth of the market that night, and what finally ended it was not persuasion.
unverified: The card's exact wording. I quote TechCrunch's version; Computerworld printed it slightly differently ("See you at MIX where we'll show..."). Attendance also varies, from "around a hundred" to "between 80 and 100".

I did not open ie6funeral.com or the original 37signals, Digg, IE6 No More and Windows blog posts (those I tried would not load), so the obituary, the 37signals notice, the Digg figures and Roger Capriotti's words are quoted from press coverage and other blogs that reproduced them.
The Digg poll result. Eric Lawrence's post adds two answers to get 69% who could not upgrade, while TechCrunch reported 77%. The poll was self-selected either way.
Everything about the YouTube banner's origin and effect rests on Chris Zacharias's own account, written ten years later, including the claim that YouTube's IE6 audience halved in a month.
The "Retiring IE6" post is signed only "Eric". I name Eric Lawrence because it is on the IEInternals blog; the page itself does not give a surname.

That the YouTube banner mostly moved home users, that IE6 Countdown's launch a year to the day after the funeral was a coincidence, and the remark about most browsers now running on Google's engine are my own inferences. I also did not open a source for Chrome's 2008 launch.

essays.title: JSConf 2009: the community that didn't know it existed
essays.description: In April 2009 about 130 people met in a hotel outside Washington for a conference about JavaScript itself. It nearly didn't happen, and its format, its side room and its name spread around the world.
unverified: Whether this was strictly the first JavaScript conference. The organizers and attendees called it that, Kevin Dangoor hedged with "possibly", and I did not search for earlier events in other countries.

The story of the mortgage-backed deposit, the drive to the hotel and the emails rests on Jan Lehnardt's 2015 speaker notes alone. Dangoor's 2010 notes confirm only that the conference was nearly cancelled and that a "sold out" notice produced a waiting list.

Who proposed taking JSConf to Europe, and when Chris Williams first raised the idea. Lehnardt and Williams each remember making the offer, and Lehnardt's 2009 post says Williams asked "last fall" while the 2015 talk places it just after RubyFringe.
The attendance figure. Dangoor wrote 130, Lehnardt "130+ attendees & speakers", and the sponsor pitch promised 125. I found no official count.
That the Ajaxian blog's founders organized The Ajax Experience. I only opened the event archive, which lists Ben Galbraith as a speaker, so the essay says no more than that.

How many editions JSConf EU held, whether JSConf US ran in every year after 2015, and who owns the JSConf name now. The sites I opened give a "10th anniversary" in 2019, a 2019 event in Carlsbad and a 2025 event "under the OpenJS Foundation", and nothing firmer.
That scarcity made community conferences harder to get into, that no library had been "the host" before, and that the job title needed the room. Those are my readings, not sourced claims.
